column2: Long hair growing on the neck of a lion or a horse; a natural hairstyle that has never once needed an appointment at the barbers.
A grate or device for cooking food over heat; the way to earn appetising stripes without so much as a frying pan.
Theatrical cosmetics and the art of altering an actor's appearance; makeup that helps one become somebody else entirely — at least until the curtain.
An acute viral infection of the airways, with fever and aching limbs; the illness that politely cancels every plan you had, including the good ones.
A hot drink of rum or another spirit with water, sugar and spices; the classic warmer of sailors — the Royal Navy's invention, and its regret ever since the rum ration went.
A weather event combining lightning, thunder and a downpour; celestial theatre with free special effects and no booking fee.
The loud crash produced by a lightning discharge; the sky's rather theatrical echo.
An old small silver coin; the classic unit of worthlessness in old English sayings — many a thing was counted as not worth one.
The upper front part of the torso; the quarters where the ribs, heart and lungs are lodged — prime real estate, sensibly protected.
Heavy goods carried for transport; anything that makes the trolley work for its living.
The upper layer of the earth's surface, and the base for building and planting; the ground beneath one's feet and, more importantly, beneath one's foundations.
A juicy fruit with a characteristically widened lower half; recognisable by silhouette alone — which is more than can be said for most of us.
A condition in which an organ or part of one pushes through a weak spot in the surrounding tissue; a diagnosis for the doctor, not for the internet.
A long, narrow elevation, or a row of something; in the garden, a tidy strip of soil for planting — tidiness optional by August.
A mixture of earth and water that spoils shoes and moods alike; the chief argument for a doormat, and the natural state of a British festival.
An opaque water-soluble paint with a dense matte finish; a medium that forgives nearly everything except a dirty brush.
A dish of meat stewed with paprika and other spices; Hungarian heartiness in a bowl — and rather better than the canteen's version.
A light cavalryman, usually in a strikingly braided uniform; dash and moustache combined in a single military silhouette.
The dense, settled part of a liquid; what remains at the bottom of the cup, to the perpetual disappointment of fortune-tellers.
A large venomous snake of arid Eurasia, kin to the adder; an encounter best declined, however warmly it is offered.
Considerable space or remoteness; everything the horizon is keeping to itself.
A courteous word for a woman, and a court card in the pack; a term with its best manners on.
An engineering structure that holds back or directs water; the earthwork standing between the river and everybody's basement.
A compulsory payment or offering to a victor or ruler; history's subscription service — automatic renewal, no refunds.
Something given freely, or a natural ability; a present from fate that sometimes insists on years of training before it works.
The designation of a calendar day, month and year; a short notation that stops one turning up a week early.
A movable structure for entering and leaving a room; the boundary between the room and the corridor — and the reason knocking was invented.
The left-hand side of a ledger account, recording inflows or increases in assets depending on the account type; the side of bookkeeping that follows rules of its own, usually noticed at year-end.
A crude insulting term, formerly used as a medical classification; in modern speech, a derogatory label best not scattered about.
A short expression of a leading idea or life principle; a phrase fit for a coat of arms and for muttering on Monday mornings.
A large seagoing vessel; a floating construction for which the horizon is merely a suggestion.
The father of one's mother or father; the senior member of the family, holder of the best armchair and the tallest stories.
The flat top or back plate of a stringed instrument's body; the surface that gives the notes their bounce — the violin's own sound system.
The head of a faculty at a university; the person in whose office timetables, examinations and departments all converge to complain.
Elements of artistic furnishing for an interior, object or space; the details by which 'adequate' quietly becomes 'rather lovely'.
Work, occupation, an act or an affair; the universal word for whatever one is engaged in — and, as the phrase goes, frequently none of yours.
A form of government in which the source of power is the people; a system in which the citizen's voice is meant to count, as the queue at the polling station proves.
The stretch between dawn and evening, or a calendar unit of 24 hours; the interval between two nights, much of which the British spend discussing the weather.
A medium of exchange, payment and accumulation; the universal go-between of desire and purchase, noted for leaving faster than it arrives.
An elected representative of citizens in a lawmaking body; a person entrusted to speak on the voters' behalf — frequently at length.
A small rural settlement; a place where, instead of traffic jams, one finds allotments, cockerels and a lively interest in everyone else's business.
A shrub or small tree of the cornel family, often grown for its ornamental leaves and bright stems; the garden's winter fireworks.
The upper layer of soil thickly interlaced with grass roots; a ready-made slice of lawn — and, in Ireland, the fuel besides.
The soft tissue surrounding the teeth and covering the jaw ridges; the part of the mouth the dentist intends to discuss every six months.
A short horizontal stroke inside a word or between its parts; a mark that joins things together but never makes a scene, unlike the dash.
A musical idiom of improvisation, syncopation and expressive rhythm; the genre in which the notes are occasionally allowed — indeed encouraged — to surprise.
A sweet mass of fruit or berries boiled with sugar; a thick preserve under no obligation to keep the fruit whole — the glory of the village fete.
A lively folk dance of Scottish or Irish origin; a rhythm at which the feet plainly know rather more than the head.
A strong alcoholic drink flavoured with juniper; the backbone of many a characterful cocktail — and, with tonic, Britain's answer to almost any question.
A spirit of Arabian mythology, able to assume many forms; a magical grantor of wishes whose small print repays careful reading.
An all-terrain vehicle; a car that promises to carry on where the tarmac loses its nerve — and frequently just past the sign saying 'ford'.
A sign in musical notation raising a note by a semitone; the little gridiron placed before the note.
A regimen of eating composed with a particular aim; a system under which the refrigerator becomes a subject for negotiations, chiefly on Friday evenings.
A semiconductor device passing current essentially in one direction only; the one-way street of electricity, with no room for a U-turn.
A flat, round object or data medium; a shape equally at home in engineering, sport and the small of one's back.
The screen of an electronic device for showing information; the surface on which the machine shares its opinions — constantly.
A young human being; the old, faintly poetic word for the small person actually in charge of the household.
Wild birds and beasts pursued by hunters; the centrepiece of a proper country-house dinner, and of rather too many country-house mysteries.
The size of a thing, or the distance from one end to the other; the measurement that answers 'how long' — and, on a motorway diversion, the answer is always 'longer'.
The lower part of the hull of a ship, a car or a container; the surface usually hidden from view — until the mechanic looks, and sighs.
The lowest inner surface of a vessel, or the lowest part of anything; the limit of depth, and sometimes of patience.
A reason offered in support of an opinion; the logical prop expected to bear the whole weight of one's position, however wobbly.
A tenet accepted as indisputable truth without proof; a conviction that declines to take questions from the floor.
Atmospheric precipitation in the form of water drops; the meteorological backbone of Britain, and a permanent reason to check where the umbrella went.
An exactly measured quantity of a medicine, substance or influence; a measure with which one is strongly advised not to improvise.
Observation or patrol for guard and control; the duty of those who may not simply go to bed like everybody else.
A port worker who loads and unloads ships; the specialist in cargoes at the quay, and the only person the crates ever obey.
A physician, or the holder of the highest academic degree; one word covering both the surgery and the senior common room — both of which will keep you waiting.
The lengthwise groove on the blade of edged weapons; a hollow that lightens the construction and changes its look — a diet for blades.
An obligation to repay money or to keep a promise; the one thing that remembers you perfectly well, calendar or no calendar.
A dwelling, or a place where one feels one belongs; the address that, in the end, matters more than any journey.
A naming area on the internet, or a self-contained field of activity; a site's address in words, sparing everyone the IP numbers.
A tall shaft furnace for smelting iron from ore; an industrial giant with a fiery appetite and no concept of office hours.
A person or organism giving blood, tissues, cells or an organ for medical purposes; the quiet hero who asks for nothing afterwards except a biscuit.
A report to the authorities about someone's actions, often with an accusatory tinge; paperwork that has ruined more relationships than gossip ever managed.
A route for vehicles and people; a strip connecting places and testing the suspension — Britain's potholes see to that.
A flat, elongated piece of wood or other material; a builder's blank and a school surface once white with chalk.
Time free from work, given over to rest and hobbies; the precious hours one intends to enjoy — frequently in a queue.
A fortified firing point of concrete or other sturdy material; the small wartime fortress that still dots the countryside, admired now chiefly by dog walkers.
Money or other values received over a period; the financial result of labour, business or investment — always quicker spent than earned.
A girl or woman in relation to her parents; the family member who may one day calmly take over the household — and the remote control.
A physical tussle between people; a debate in which the arguments have been replaced by fists and the conclusion by bruises.
Slow movement under the action of current, wind or other forces; travel without a course of one's own — a national motoring style, some say.
A power tool or hand implement for boring holes; the device that turns a wall into a colander, invariably on a Sunday morning.
A state of light half-sleep; the pleasant stretch between wakefulness and proper sleep, best enjoyed in front of the television.
Involuntary rhythmic trembling of the body or its parts; the reaction to cold, fear or strong excitement — in Britain, overwhelmingly the first.
A songbird of the Turdidae family; the woodland musician, famed for its voice — the bird Thomas Hardy trusted to sing at the year's end.
A shrub with yellow flowers, some species grown as ornamentals; the plant from which an English royal house borrowed its very name.
A large steppe bird, among the heaviest of flying birds; a dweller of open spaces, happily back on Salisbury Plain after a long English absence.
A close person bound by trust and mutual support; the one you may telephone without an occasion — at any hour, regrettably.
An intergrowth of crystals on a common base; a natural composition no designer had to assemble — nature showing off, in fact.
A priest and scholar of the ancient Celts; keeper of rites and learning in pre-Christian Europe — and, at the solstice, of white robes at Stonehenge.
A second copy or a repeat; in cinema another take, in sport a repeated feat — and, at the bar, an order worth specifying clearly.
A curved line resembling part of a circle; a bend met in geometry and in the rainbow — the rainbow being the pleasanter assignment.
A simple wind instrument, a tube with holes; music that fits in a pocket — and, in the right hands, empties towns of rats.
A curved part joining or holding pieces of an object together; for example, the bit of one's spectacles that hooks over the ear — and the first bit to need mending.
An old gold coin widespread in Europe; money from the era when a purse could jingle honestly with gold.
The front end of a firearm's barrel, through which the projectile leaves; the opening it is wise never to argue with.
A cavity inside a tree trunk or a large branch; nature's own pied-à-terre for birds and beasts.
In religious and philosophical thought, the immaterial essence of a person; figuratively, the whole inner world — occasionally mislaid, never quite lost.
A combat between two opponents under established rules, historically often in defence of honour; disagreement settled at dawn, with seconds present and honour satisfied.
A performance by two, or a piece for two voices or instruments; a musical conversation for two — provided both parties let the other finish.
A suspension of fine particles and gases arising from combustion; the visible trace of fire — and, in Britain, the traditional excuse to step outside.
A sweet, fragrant fruit of a gourd plant with juicy flesh; the summer treat that smells delicious long before the knife comes out.
An opening or gap in a surface; an absence of material exactly where material was wanted.
A spout or narrowed channel directing a flow of liquid or gas; the technical exit through which the stream departs.
A unit of length equal to 2.54 centimetres; a measure still used for screens and pipes, and Britain's final 2.54 centimetres of resistance to the metric system.
A hill of sand created by the wind; a mountain that reshapes itself without a single machine — the envy of every building site.
The brother of one's mother or father; the relative guaranteed a leading role in every family story, usually one involving fish, or the war.
A woodland bird with a stout bill, hammering bark in search of insects; nature's drummer — keeping time, if not the neighbours' approval.
A specialist in the protection and management of a hunting estate; the woodland worker who knows the ground better than any map — and, some say, than the landlord.
Nourishment eaten to sustain the body; the necessary pleasure around which markets and family conversations are equally built.
Travel by vehicle or on horseback; a process in which the route, the speed and a certain caution all have their parts to play.
One who rides on horseback or controls a vehicle; a participant in the journey rather than merely luggage that steers.
An evergreen conifer with short needles and drooping cones; the forest beauty dressed up once a year — and, as it happens, tidy by name as well as by nature.
